definition: The broad field of building computer systems that perform tasks we usually associate with human intelligence, such as understanding language or recognising images.
Systematic unfairness in a model's output, usually inherited from gaps or skews in its training data.
The maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can take into account at once, including your prompt and its reply.
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. It powers most modern image, speech and language AI.
Extra training of an existing model on a smaller, focused dataset so it gets better at a particular task or style.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio or code, rather than only classifying existing content.
When a model produces an answer that sounds confident and plausible but is false or made up.
A very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. Chat assistants are built on LLMs.
An approach to AI where a program learns patterns from example data instead of following hand-written rules.
The trained result of a machine learning process: a file of learned numbers plus the code that uses them to make predictions.
A model made of layers of simple connected maths units, loosely inspired by neurons in the brain.
The internal numbers a model adjusts during training. Large language models have billions of them.
The instructions or question you give a generative AI model.
A chunk of text, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark, that a language model reads and writes.
The examples a model learns from. Its quality and coverage strongly shape what the model can do and how it fails.
